title: Trapping Rain Water
description: Total units of water retained between an elevation profile's bars.
statement:
An elevation profile is given as a row of bars whose widths are all one unit.

Rain falls and settles between the bars. Report the total number of units of water the profile can hold.

Above bar `i`, the water level can rise no higher than the shorter of the tallest bar on its left and the tallest bar on its right, so the units held there are `min(left_max, right_max) - height[i]`. Bars at the ends never hold water because one side has no bar at all.

Computing both maxima from scratch would be quadratic; a two-pointer sweep that always advances the shorter of the two current bars keeps the accumulated maximum on the other side already known, making the whole pass linear.
inputFormat:
The input is read from standard input as exactly two lines:

1. Line 1: integer `n` - the number of bars (`0 <= n <= 10^5`).
2. Line 2: `n` space-separated integers `height[0] ... height[n-1]`. When `n` is 0 this line is empty.
outputFormat: Print a single line containing the total number of trapped water units as a single integer (`0` when fewer than two bars are given).
constraints: All bars are one unit wide
The total can exceed a 32-bit integer (up to about 10^10), so use a 64-bit accumulator
notes: `n = 0`, `n = 1` and `n = 2` all hold 0 units, because the end bars always leak. A monotonically rising or falling profile holds nothing at all. Do not clamp the per-bar contribution at zero by accident - it is never negative, since the accumulated maximum on the processed side is always at least the current bar's height. The 64-bit accumulator matters: a 100000-bar profile traps far more than 2^31.

Step 2: the tallest bar in this profile is the 3 at index 7, so for every position before it the right-hand limit is 3 and the left-hand limit comes from the tallest bar seen so far.
Step 3: filling in the units per index gives 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0.
Step 4: index 2 fills up to 1 because of the bar of height 1 at index 1, and index 5 fills up to 2 because of the bar of height 2 at index 3.
Step 5: the contributions are 1 (index 2) + 1 (index 4) + 2 (index 5) + 1 (index 6) + 1 (index 9) = 6.

Step 1: heights 4 and 5 are the outer walls.
Step 2: index 1 (height 2) is bounded by the wall of 4 on its left and the wall of 5 on its right, so it holds `min(4, 5) - 2 = 2` units.
Step 3: index 2 (height 0) holds `min(4, 5) - 0 = 4` units.
Step 4: index 3 (height 3) holds `min(4, 5) - 3 = 1` unit, and index 4 (height 2) holds 2.
Step 5: the total is 2 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 9.

Step 1: the bars are 3, 0, 2, 0, 4, so the leftmost and rightmost bars leak and hold nothing.
Step 2: index 1 (height 0) is bounded by the bar of 3 on its left and the bar of 4 on its right, so it holds `min(3, 4) - 0 = 3` units.
Step 3: index 2 (height 2) is also bounded by 3 and 4, so it holds `3 - 2 = 1` unit.
Step 4: index 3 (height 0) is bounded by 3 and 4 as well, so it holds `3 - 0 = 3` units.
Step 5: the total is 3 + 1 + 3 = 7.
